newsitem.title: USA: DC mayor proposes $5 bln balanced budget for city.
newsitem.headline: DC mayor proposes $5 bln balanced budget for city.

text.p: District of Columbia Mayor Marion Barry on Monday proposed a $5 billion balanced budget for the struggling city in fiscal 1998, but D.C.'s congressionally appointed CFO said the plan does not have his or the D.C. financial control board's approval.
A major issue is Barry's proposal to save $50 million next year by restructuring outstanding city debt, according to a 320-page budget document released today.
The proposal now goes to the city's five-member control board which hopes to send a final budget proposal to Congress for approval by the end of March.

In a letter accompanying the proposed budget, Chief Financial Officer Anthony Williams warned Barry that restructuring city debt without resolving massive problems like the city's unfunded pension liability first will be "poorly received" by Wall Street.
Williams is bracing for the results of an independent audit of fiscal 1996 city finances by KPMG Peat Marwick this week that does not give D.C. finances a clean bill of health.
D.C. is not required by Congress to balance its budget until fiscal 1999.

But D.C. and its five-member control board want to balance it in fiscal 1998 to impress Congress, which will begin reviewing a $3.9 billion, five-year federal relief package for D.C. developed by the White House.
Williams said that, overall, Barry's plan is "conservative" and "preserves key priorities" held by him, the city's control board and city council.
In an unusual tactic, the document gives Congress a "snapshot" of four other budget scenarios that Williams, the city's council and the control board are developing.
But none of the alternatives to Barry's plan add up to a balanced budget yet, the document says.
This is "the first working draft of a balanced FY 1998 budget" and is still a "work in progress," Barry stressed in a budget transmittal letter to the control board.

Noting that his budget's primary focus is economic development, Barry said he will declare nearly three city wards east of the Anacostia River a development zone. He said he will "coordinate resources" to develop the region.
Barry said he will continue to reduce the city's workforce through restructuring, streamlining and outsourcing services that the city can no longer afford to offer.
Barry said he knows that a proposal he made two years ago to restructure city debt was rejected because his administration had not shown a willingness to downsize city government.
But, since then, D.C. has "conducted one of the most complex transformations and downsizing of any local government," Barry said.
He said debt restructuring is critical in order to balance the city's budget one year earlier than Congress required.
